spec: Word-wrap a string of space-separated words into a list of lines, each at most width characters long, without splitting any word across lines. Words are joined with single spaces. An empty string produces an empty list. Assume no single word is longer than width.
visible_tests: assert wrap_text('the quick brown fox', 10) == ['the quick', 'brown fox']
assert wrap_text('one two three four', 7) == ['one two', 'three', 'four']

spec: Given a list of words and a target width, produce a single justified line where the words exactly fill the width by distributing extra spaces between them as evenly as possible, with any leftover spaces going into the leftmost gaps first. If there is only one word, left-justify it within the width. Assume width is always achievable.
Given a list of value strings and a column width, right-align each value within that width and join them with the separator ' | '.

Word-wrap a string of space-separated words at a maximum line width (without splitting words) and return the number of lines the wrapped text would occupy. An empty string requires zero lines. Assume no single word is longer than width.

Arrange a list of string items into rows of a fixed number of columns, left-justifying each item to a given width and joining items in a row with a single space; the last row may contain fewer than ncols items. Return the list of row strings. An empty item list returns an empty list.

Truncate a string to at most maxlen characters, replacing the final characters with '...' if truncation is needed so the result is exactly maxlen characters long. If the string already fits, return it unchanged. If maxlen is 3 or less, just hard-truncate to maxlen characters without adding an ellipsis.

Keep only the first maxwords whitespace-separated words of a string, joined by single spaces, and append '...' if there were more words than maxwords. If the string has maxwords or fewer words, return it re-joined with single spaces and no ellipsis.
visible_tests: assert truncate_words_ellipsis('the quick brown fox', 2) == 'the quick...'
assert truncate_words_ellipsis('one two three', 3) == 'one two three'

spec: Shorten a string to exactly maxlen characters by keeping characters from the start and end and replacing the middle portion with '...', keeping the start slightly longer than the end when the remaining length is odd. If the string already fits within maxlen, return it unchanged.

Return the initials of a full name with a period after each letter, taking the first letter of each whitespace-separated word, uppercased, joined with no extra separator between the period and the next initial. Assume the name has at least one word.

Given a full name of two or more whitespace-separated words, abbreviate the first word to its initial followed by a period, and keep the remaining words unchanged, joined by single spaces. If the name has only one word, return it unchanged.
Build a traditional three-letter monogram from a first, middle, and last name, given as separate non-empty strings: the result is the uppercase initials in the order first, last, middle.
Given a first name, middle name, and last name as separate non-empty strings, return them formatted as 'First M. Last' where M is the uppercase initial of the middle name.

Given a full name of one or more whitespace-separated words, if there is more than one word, move the last word to the front followed by a comma, keeping the remaining words in order; if there is only one word, return it unchanged.
visible_tests: assert reverse_name('Ada Marie Lovelace') == 'Lovelace, Ada Marie'

spec: Given a full name of one or more whitespace-separated words, keep only the first and last words (dropping any middle names), joined by a single space. If the name has one or two words, return it unchanged (words joined by a single space).
Convert a camelCase or PascalCase string into a lowercase hyphen-separated slug by inserting a hyphen before every internal uppercase letter and lowercasing the whole result.

Convert a string into a slug the same way as ordinary slugification but using underscores instead of hyphens as the separator: lowercase the text, replace every run of characters that are not lowercase letters or digits with a single underscore, and strip leading/trailing underscores.

Given a base slug string and a list of already-taken slug strings, return the base slug if it is not in the taken list; otherwise return the base slug suffixed with '-2', '-3', and so on, using the smallest suffix number starting at 2 that is not already taken.
Convert a space-separated title string into a hashtag by capitalizing the first letter of every word and concatenating them with no spaces, prefixed with '#'.
Convert a snake_case string (words separated by underscores) into PascalCase, capitalizing every word and removing the underscores.
Convert a PascalCase string into snake_case by inserting an underscore before every internal uppercase letter and lowercasing the whole result.
Convert a kebab-case string (words separated by hyphens) into camelCase, where the first word stays lowercase and every subsequent word is capitalized, with all hyphens removed.
Convert a camelCase string into kebab-case by inserting a hyphen before every internal uppercase letter and lowercasing the whole result.
Convert a space-separated, title-cased phrase into snake_case by lowercasing each word and joining them with underscores.
Convert a space-separated phrase into PascalCase by capitalizing each word and concatenating them with no separator.
Convert a string with words separated by spaces, hyphens, or underscores into CONSTANT_CASE: uppercase every word and join them with underscores.
Format an integer as a string with commas separating groups of three digits, keeping a leading minus sign for negative numbers in front of the separated digits.
Format a number as US currency: two decimal places, comma thousands separators, and a leading dollar sign, with the minus sign (if the amount is negative) placed before the dollar sign.
Convert a fraction (e.g. 0.5) into a percentage string with exactly one decimal place and a trailing percent sign (e.g. '50.0%'). Negative fractions and fractions above 1 are formatted the same way.
Format a number as a string with exactly the given number of decimal places.

Convert a non-negative number of whole seconds into a string. If the duration is under one hour, format it as 'M:SS' (minutes, no leading zero, and two-digit seconds). If it is one hour or more, format it as 'H:MM:SS'.

Append the correct English ordinal suffix ('st', 'nd', 'rd', or 'th') to an integer, based on its last one or two digits: numbers ending in 11, 12, or 13 always use 'th'; otherwise numbers ending in 1, 2, or 3 use 'st', 'nd', 'rd' respectively, and all others use 'th'. Negative numbers use the suffix for their absolute value.
Format an integer with an explicit sign: prefix positive numbers with '+', leave negative numbers as-is (with their existing minus sign), and format zero as the plain string '0' with no sign.
Given a positive integer numerator and denominator, reduce the fraction to lowest terms using their greatest common divisor and return it as a string 'a/b'.
Convert an integer between 1 and 3999 inclusive into its Roman numeral representation using standard subtractive notation.
Given a numeric card number string of at least 4 digits, mask all digits except the last four with asterisks, then group the resulting characters into blocks of four separated by single spaces.
Format a Celsius temperature value as a string with exactly one decimal place followed by the degree Celsius symbol '°C'.

Pluralize an English noun using simple rules: words ending in s, x, z, ch, or sh get 'es' appended; words ending in a consonant followed by y have the y replaced with 'ies'; all other words simply get 's' appended.

Format a count with a noun, using the singular form of the word when the count is exactly 1 and otherwise pluralizing it with simple English rules (s/x/z/ch/sh get 'es', consonant+y becomes 'ies', otherwise add 's'), producing a string like '3 cats'.

Convert a simple plural English noun back to its likely singular form: words ending in 'ies' (with more than 3 letters) become 'y'; words ending in 'ses', 'xes', 'zes', 'ches', or 'shes' drop the trailing 'es'; other words ending in 's' (but not 'ss') drop the final 's'; anything else is returned unchanged.
Given a count and explicit singular and plural word forms, return a string combining the count with the singular form when the count is exactly 1, or the plural form otherwise.
